narrative:
The model predicted an 84.9% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess risk, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, both pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Being in the bottom decile in both years—one compared to an average of about 6 among accepted students—signaled consistent academic struggle relative to your peers. This was the dominant reason the model saw high risk.

Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 3.60, it is noticeably higher than the 3.23 average among accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction somewhat toward success. However, this positive signal was not strong enough to overcome the negative impact of your class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 27, well below the 37 average of accepted students, and your middle family income bracket also contributed to the overall picture, though less decisively than your school performance.

To improve your chances in the future, focus on strengthening your academic standing. Retaking the LSAT to raise your score significantly, or completing additional coursework that demonstrates sustained high performance, would help show the model a clearer path to passing the bar. Consider reapplying once you have concrete evidence of improvement. (248 words)
